title: Vulnerability to Dams of the Last Undammed Large Rivers of Southeast Asia
content:
ABSTRACT

The vast majority of large Eurasian rivers are regulated by hydropower dams, but some have survived as free-flowing rivers so far in the Arctic and along stretches of the Myanmar coast. There, the Ayeyarwady (Irrawaddy) and Salween Rivers, two of the largest rivers of Southeast Asia, provide a huge amount of sediment, nurturing floodplains and deltas and play a unique role in national food security and other socioeconomic and environmental services. Over the past 40 years, Southeast Asia has experienced intense land-use changes, including deforestation and mining, alongside the rapid expansion of hydropower infrastructure. The region studied here is marked by conflict and political instability, which partly explains why these rivers remain largely free of such infrastructure. Using a method initially applied in the Amazon basin, we assess the environmental condition of four rivers—Ayeyarwady (Irrawaddy), Sittaung, Bilin and Salween—through the lens of hydropower dam development. We highlight the status and preservation of these basins while showing how planned projects could affect their hydrosystems. The Sittaung basin, already saturated by dams, would change little, with nearly 50% of its river network already disconnected. By contrast, the Ayeyarwady basin, still relatively well preserved with about 75% of the basin's whole river lengths free-flowing, could lose roughly half of that connectivity. The Salween would be the most affected: although about 75% of its river length is currently free-flowing, this proportion could fall to 8%. Most electricity generated by these projects would be exported to neighbouring countries, contributing less to Myanmar's development and even less to the communities directly affected.
